name: Estate of Hernandez v. City of Los Angeles
court: Ninth Circuit, en banc (from the Central District of California)
citation: No. 21-55994 (9th Cir. June 2, 2025) (en banc), cert. denied, No. 25-538 (U.S. June 22, 2026)
topic: Deadly force against a man with a box cutter advancing on an officer after commands; three volleys in six seconds; duty to reassess after the suspect falls; qualified immunity under Zion v. County of Orange
summary: An LAPD officer at a chaotic crash scene shot a man six times in about six seconds as he advanced on her with a box cutter and ignored repeated commands to stop and drop it. The en banc Ninth Circuit held that the first two volleys were reasonable as a matter of law, but that a jury could find the third volley, fired after the man had fallen and was rolling away on the ground, unreasonable, and that Zion v. County of Orange clearly established that an officer must reassess rather than continue shooting a fallen suspect who no longer appears to be a threat. Five judges dissented from the qualified immunity ruling. The Supreme Court denied certiorari. It is taught for the reassessment duty and for the limits of that duty.

June 2, 2025) (en banc) (F.4th citation not confirmed from the sources read), cert. denied sub nom. City of Los Angeles v. Estate of Hernandez, No. 25-538 (U.S. June 22, 2026).
facts:
The facts are as the en banc majority stated them, relying on the officer's body camera, her vehicle camera, and a bystander's phone video, with ambiguities resolved in the plaintiffs' favor. The dissents read the video differently on several points, noted below.

Late on the afternoon of April 22, 2020, Los Angeles Police Department Officers Toni McBride and Shuhei Fuchigami came upon a multi vehicle collision on San Pedro Street. Four vehicles were damaged, including a black truck that had struck a parked RV, and at least 25 people had gathered, some screaming. As the officers got out, the radio reported that the suspect was male and armed with a knife. Bystanders pointed to the black truck and said a crazy guy with a knife was inside threatening to kill himself; one said he had caused the accident. McBride drew her Glock 17 to the low ready, told Fuchigami to call for backup, and cleared bystanders from the area. The radio added that the suspect was cutting himself inside his vehicle. McBride asked whether they had less lethal options; she carried pepper spray and a taser and knew a 40 millimeter launcher was in the patrol vehicle.

McBride saw the man, Daniel Hernandez, rummaging in the center console and then climbing out the far window. She called out for him to show his hands. About six seconds later he came around the rear of the truck roughly 43 feet from her, shirtless and sweating heavily, holding something in his right hand that turned out to be a box cutter, and began walking toward her. McBride backed up about ten feet along a stopped Camry, gestured for him to stop, and ordered him to stay there and drop the knife. He kept coming. She ordered him twice more to drop the knife. Hernandez raised his extended arms to about 45 degrees at his sides and, according to the majority, said nothing; the dissents say the video shows him yelling. McBride pointed her gun at him. He took three more steps, closing to about 36 feet. She yelled "Drop it!" and fired two rounds.

Hernandez fell on his right side and yelled out. He rolled onto his hands and knees facing down and began to push himself up, though he did not continue toward her. McBride again yelled to drop it and fired two more rounds. He fell onto his back and, in the majority's description, curled into a ball with his knees against his chest and his arms around them; the dissents say he was moving and rolling the entire time, got onto his elbow and knee, and appeared to be trying to rise. As he rolled away from McBride onto his left side she fired two more rounds. He collapsed and remained down. The whole sequence took about 6.2 seconds: about 2.5 seconds between the first and second volleys and about 1.4 seconds between the second and third. The box cutter was still in his hand when another officer removed it. The sixth shot caused an immediately fatal head wound; the fourth shot damaged his lung and liver and may have been survivable. Other officers arrived only after the shooting began.

The Los Angeles Board of Police Commissioners found that McBride acted outside LAPD lethal force policy in firing the fifth and sixth rounds, because after the second volley Hernandez had not repositioned himself to resume an advance.

Hernandez's parents and minor daughter sued McBride, the LAPD, and the city under 42 U.S.C. section 1983 for excessive force, municipal liability, and interference with familial relations, and under California law for assault, battery, wrongful death, and the Bane Act. The district court granted summary judgment to the defendants on every claim, finding the force reasonable and alternatively finding qualified immunity. A three judge panel held the final two shots presented a triable issue but that McBride was entitled to qualified immunity. The Ninth Circuit reheard the case en banc.
holding:
Affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded. Judge Nguyen wrote for the en banc majority.

The first two volleys were reasonable as a matter of law. When McBride began firing she had probable cause to believe Hernandez had caused a serious collision, saw him advancing with a bladed weapon, and knew he had refused commands to stop and drop it, which created heightened urgency and unpredictability. A reasonable officer could conclude he threatened her and the bystanders. The court rejected the argument that Deorle v. Rutherford required a different approach because Hernandez was apparently emotionally disturbed; Deorle involved an unarmed man and officers who had time, and Hernandez fell more closely into the category of an armed and dangerous person who had recently committed a serious offense. The court also rejected the argument that McBride should have kept retreating, used cover, waited until he was in striking range, or used less lethal options, citing Scott v. Henrich for the rule that officers need not use the least intrusive means and Lal v. California for the rule that officers need not endanger their own lives by allowing a suspect to continue a dangerous course merely because he may be intent on suicide by police. After the first volley Hernandez reoriented toward McBride and rose halfway to standing while ignoring another command, so a reasonable officer could conclude he still presented an imminent threat when she fired the third and fourth rounds, though the court called that a closer question.

The third volley is for the jury. Under Plumhoff, officers justified in firing need not stop until the threat has ended, but it is a different case if a second round of shots follows an initial round that has clearly incapacitated the suspect. Under Zion, terminating a threat does not necessarily mean terminating the suspect; if the suspect is on the ground and appears wounded he may no longer pose a threat, and a reasonable officer would reassess rather than continue shooting. Viewing the video in the plaintiffs' favor, after the second volley Hernandez was on his back, rolling away, well beyond striking distance, armed only with a melee weapon, and writhing from four gunshot wounds; it was not clear he would or could get up. McBride had her gun trained on him and had already knocked him down twice. She had an obligation to reassess before continuing to fire, and a jury could find her failure to do so unreasonable. The court said Wilkinson v. Torres did not authorize officers to shoot mindlessly until the suspect was dead but recognized that officers may need to reevaluate after each shot if circumstances permit. It rejected the dissent's position that six seconds is too short as a matter of law, saying continued force against an armed suspect is not per se reasonable because he is still moving, and that whether a threat perceptibly ended is a factual question ordinarily ill suited for summary judgment.

Clearly established. By 2020 Zion had clearly established for several years that an officer cannot continue shooting a suspect who is on the ground, appears wounded, and shows no signs of getting up without first reassessing, particularly when the suspect has a knife rather than a firearm. The defendants did not contest that rule; they disputed its factual premise. The court held Zion squarely controls: there, after a justified first volley, the officer fired a second volley at a fallen suspect who was still moving but making no threatening gestures, and the court distinguished nonthreatening movements from an attempt to get up. Here a jury could find Hernandez's movements after the second volley were due to pain and were nonthreatening, and that McBride could have protected herself by keeping her gun on him and firing only if he attempted to flee or attack. The court said whether Zion still held his knife was a red herring; the distance here, about 36 feet, meant possession of a bladed weapon did not present an immediate threat if he was not trying to get up. McBride was therefore not entitled to qualified immunity, and summary judgment on the Fourth Amendment claim was reversed.

Remaining claims. Because the district court dismissed the state law claims solely for lack of a Fourth Amendment violation, that ruling was reversed. The court adopted the panel's discussion affirming summary judgment on the municipal liability claim and the Fourteenth Amendment familial integrity claims.

The Supreme Court denied the city's petition for certiorari on June 22, 2026; Justices Thomas and Alito would have granted it.
notDecided:
Whether McBride's fifth and sixth shots were in fact unreasonable. The court held only that a jury could so find; the case was remanded for trial on that question.

Whether the first four shots could be challenged. The court held them reasonable as a matter of law, and the plaintiffs cannot recover for them.

Whether McBride violated California law. The state law claims were reinstated only because the district court had dismissed them on the Fourth Amendment ruling; the court did not analyze them. Judge Nelson's separate opinion would have affirmed their dismissal and noted that California negligence law can be broader than the Fourth Amendment.

Municipal liability and the familial integrity claims. Summary judgment for the defendants on those claims was affirmed by adopting the panel's analysis. Judge Nelson's opinion argued the circuit should reexamine whether parents of adult children and children of parents have substantive due process companionship rights at all; the majority did not take up that question.

Whether Zion should be overruled. Judge Bumatay urged that; the majority did not address it.

The denial of certiorari is not a Supreme Court ruling on the merits.
inPractice:
Hernandez is the Ninth Circuit's most detailed statement of two rules that pull in opposite directions, and an officer needs both.

The first rule favors the officer. An officer facing a person who advances with a bladed weapon, ignores commands to stop and drop it, and has apparently already hurt people may use deadly force before the person is within striking range, need not keep retreating or wait for a less lethal tool that is not in hand, and need not hold fire because the person may be emotionally disturbed or suicidal. Eleven judges agreed that the first two volleys here were reasonable as a matter of law. That is the deadly force baseline from Garner, Scott v. Henrich, Blanford, and Lal.

The second rule limits the first. Once shots have put the person on the ground, the justification does not run on its own. If the person appears wounded and is not trying to get up, the officer must reassess before firing again; the gun stays on the person and the trigger is pulled only if he tries to rise, attack, or flee. The court said the suspect still moving is not by itself enough to keep shooting, and distance matters: at 36 feet a man on the ground with a box cutter is not an immediate threat unless he is getting up. The LAPD's own Board of Police Commissioners reached the same conclusion under department policy before the court did.

The disagreement among the judges is itself the practical lesson. Four judges thought no reasonable officer could be expected to reassess in 1.4 seconds while an armed man kept moving, five concluded the law was not clearly established, and Judge Bumatay said the majority had adopted an extreme version of the moment of threat rule that Barnes v. Felix rejected. Two Supreme Court Justices would have taken the case. Officers should not plan around the hope that the dissents will become the law. The safer course, and the one department policy already required, is to fire, assess, and fire again only if the threat is still there.

Dr. Sowards teaches Hernandez in the deadly force line for the reassessment point and alongside Barnes for how the timeline is analyzed.
trainIt:
Teach the three volley structure because the court did. Put the sequence on a timeline: commands and retreat, first volley at 36 feet as the man advances, fall, man rolls to hands and knees and begins to rise while ignoring another command, second volley about 2.5 seconds after the first, man on his back rolling away, third volley 1.4 seconds later. Have students identify at each volley what the threat indicators were. The court found indicators present at volleys one and two (advancing, armed, noncompliant, then rising) and found a jury question at volley three (on the ground, rolling away, 36 feet off, no attempt to rise on the plaintiffs' reading).

Teach reassessment as a trained skill, not a legal abstraction. The majority said an officer in McBride's position could protect herself by keeping her weapon on the fallen man and firing only if he attempted to flee or attack. Drill that: shoot to stop, come off the trigger, assess, verbalize, and be ready to shoot again. The dissents worried that the ruling discourages pauses; the training answer is that the pause is a trained behavior performed with the weapon on target, which is what the court said a reasonable officer would do.

Teach the baseline honestly. The court held as a matter of law that shooting an armed man advancing at 36 feet after repeated commands was reasonable, that the officer did not have to keep retreating, use cover, or wait for the 40 millimeter launcher, and that the man's apparent disturbance did not change that. Students should not leave thinking Hernandez requires hesitation at the start of the encounter.

Teach the dissents as a warning about video. Judges Nelson and Collins read the same footage frame by frame and saw a man trying to get up; the majority saw convulsive movement. Officers should expect their shootings to be reviewed this way and should articulate, in reports and statements, what they saw the person doing at each moment they fired.

Teach the policy point. The Board of Police Commissioners found the final two shots out of policy before any court ruled. Department policy on reassessment is the standard officers will be measured against first.
caution: Read in full from the Ninth Circuit's website. The en banc opinion is published and binding in the Ninth Circuit; certiorari was denied June 22, 2026 with two Justices voting to grant, and that denial is not a merits ruling. The court held that a jury could find the final two shots unreasonable and that qualified immunity does not apply; no jury has found that McBride used excessive force, and the first four shots were held reasonable as a matter of law. The majority and the dissents disagree about what the video shows after the second volley; this brief reports both readings. The F.4th citation for the en banc opinion was not confirmed. The brief does not analyze the state law claims, which the court reinstated without deciding.
dissent:
Three separate opinions, representing five of the eleven judges on the qualified immunity question. Judge R. Nelson, joined by Judges Bress and Bumatay and in part by Judge Bade, would have held that McBride never violated the Fourth Amendment. In his view Plumhoff controls: officers justified in firing need not stop until the threat has ended, and six shots in six seconds at an armed man who was rising and never stopped moving did not trigger any duty to reassess, let alone two. He said the majority's analysis turned on a 0.63 second difference between pauses it treated as insignificant and a pause it treated as creating a duty, read Wilkinson backwards, and would push officers to keep shooting rather than pause. He would have affirmed dismissal of the state law claims, noting no party had argued how California's standards diverge, and he argued the circuit should reexamine whether parents of adult children and children of parents have substantive due process companionship rights under Washington v. Glucksberg.

Judge Collins, who authored the panel opinion, agreed that the first four shots were reasonable as a matter of law and that a jury could find the last two unreasonable, and he concurred in reinstating the state law claims. But joined by four other judges he dissented on qualified immunity. He said Zion is materially distinguishable on its own terms: Zion resolved for the jury whether the suspect was trying to get up, whether he still had the knife, and whether the officer thought he was armed, while here the video shows Hernandez continuously moving in a way that objectively appeared to be an attempt to rise, still holding his weapon, with the officer still commanding him to drop it. He criticized the majority for framing the clearly established rule at a high level of generality and for relying on the Zion briefing and oral argument rather than what the Zion opinion said, which he said leaves officers unable to rely on the text of the court's opinions.

Judge Bumatay joined Judge Nelson and wrote separately that the majority had adopted an extreme version of the moment of threat rule that the Supreme Court rejected in Barnes v. Felix, by ignoring everything but the last 1.4 seconds, and that the court should have overruled Zion.

applications.title: The first volleys were reasonable as a matter of law
applications.body: An armed man advancing at 36 feet after repeated commands to stop and drop a blade, who had apparently already caused a serious crash, could lawfully be shot. The officer did not have to keep retreating, use cover, wait for a launcher, or hold fire because he seemed disturbed or suicidal.

applications.title: Reassess when the person is down
applications.body: If shots have put the person on the ground and he appears wounded and is not trying to get up, a reasonable officer reassesses rather than continuing to fire. Keep the weapon on him and fire again only if he tries to rise, attack, or flee.

applications.title: Still moving is not the same as still a threat
applications.body: The court held that continued force against an armed suspect is not automatically reasonable because he is still moving, and that at 36 feet a man on the ground with a bladed weapon is not an immediate threat unless he is getting up.

applications.title: Policy got there first
applications.body: The Board of Police Commissioners found the fifth and sixth shots out of policy because Hernandez had not repositioned to resume an advance. Department reassessment policy is the first standard an officer will be measured against.

applications.title: Expect frame by frame review
applications.body: Eleven judges watched the same video, disagreed about what it showed after the second volley, and divided six to five on qualified immunity. Articulate what you saw the person doing at each moment you fired, and train to make that articulation accurate.

quiz.q: What did the en banc Ninth Circuit hold about Officer McBride's first two volleys of shots?
options: They were unreasonable because Hernandez was 36 feet away
They were reasonable as a matter of law because Hernandez was advancing with a bladed weapon, ignoring commands, after apparently causing a serious collision
They were reasonable only because other officers had arrived
quiz.teach: The court held the first four shots reasonable as a matter of law, rejected arguments that McBride should have kept retreating or waited for less lethal options, and said Hernandez's apparent disturbance did not change the analysis.

quiz.q: Why did the court hold that the third volley presented a triable issue?
options: Because any shot after the first is presumptively excessive
Because Hernandez had dropped the box cutter

Because, viewing the video in the plaintiffs' favor, Hernandez was on his back rolling away, well beyond striking distance, and not shown to be trying to get up, so a jury could find McBride had to reassess before firing again
Because the officer fired too quickly in the first volley
quiz.teach: Under Zion, a suspect on the ground who appears wounded may no longer be a threat, and a reasonable officer reassesses rather than continuing to shoot. The court said whether the threat perceptibly ended is ordinarily a jury question.

quiz.q: What was the central disagreement between the majority and Judge Collins on qualified immunity?
options: Whether deadly force was justified at the start of the encounter
Whether Zion squarely governs facts where the suspect kept moving in a way that appeared to be an attempt to rise and still held his weapon
Whether the Fourth Amendment applies to shootings
Whether the state law claims should be reinstated
quiz.teach: The majority held Zion squarely controls and that a jury could find Hernandez's movements nonthreatening. Judge Collins, joined by four judges, said Zion is materially distinguishable on its own facts and the majority defined the rule at too high a level of generality.
